clue.text: Where are you going in old Rome?…

definitions.text: Where are you going in old Rome?

parts.words: Where are you going in old Rome?
parts.note: the question as an ancient Roman would ask it, that is, the Latin words for it, famous as a novel and film title

explanation.surface: A traveller asks what a Roman citizen would say to someone setting off.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue asks for the Latin of 'Where are you going?', the words Peter is said to have spoken to Christ outside Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase translates literally as the English question, so it is what a Roman speaker would say.

clue.text: Game leaves ring inside

indicators.note: inside says the ring shape sits within the word meaning leaves

parts.note: someone who leaves a job quits
O is a ring because of its shape

explanation.surface: A player walks out, leaving a ring indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' puts O, a ring by its shape, within QUITS.
explanation.definitionFit: Quoits is a game of throwing rings at a peg.

clue.text: The mark of something corrupt

parts.note: editors of old manuscripts put a sign beside a passage they believe has been corrupted in copying

explanation.surface: A telltale sign of dishonesty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corrupt' suggests bribery, but here it means a spurious passage in a text, which scholars marked with a dagger or a dash.
explanation.definitionFit: The obelus is the sign, a dash or dagger, set against suspect or spurious text in ancient manuscripts.

clue.text: Change coats for the races

indicators.note: change tells us to alter the arrangement of the letters of coats

explanation.surface: Putting on a different jacket to go racing.
explanation.walkthrough: ASCOT is the racecourse in Berkshire, home of Royal Ascot, a famous fashion occasion.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a racecourse and its race meeting, so going to Ascot is going to the races.

clue.text: Ted's in a … in a tizzy, acting as substitute

indicators.note: in a tizzy means flustered and confused, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: Ted's is read as Ted plus S, the possessive letter counted

explanation.surface: Ted gets flustered when standing in for someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a tizzy' rearranges TEDS, IN and A. The dots suggest a missing word, but the fodder is all there.
explanation.definitionFit: Instead means in place of another, which is how a stand-in or replacement serves.

clue.text: …being British abroad, going back

indicators.note: abroad here means scattered all over, so the letters of the words beside it are spread into a new order

explanation.surface: Following the Latin question, a Brit overseas is heading home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abroad' rearranges BEING plus B into the answer. The leading dots tie this clue to 1 Across, as if the Roman question were put to a Briton travelling.
explanation.definitionFit: The tide retreating is said to ebb, so something ebbing is receding or going back.

clue.text: Not very outstanding sculpture

parts.note: outstanding is read literally as standing out from the surface, and this carving barely does

explanation.surface: A dismissive review of a mediocre statue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outstanding' looks like praise, but it means projecting: low relief carving stands only slightly proud of its background.
explanation.definitionFit: Bas-relief is French for low relief, carving whose figures project only slightly from the background.

clue.text: Not published it — indeed not so

indicators.note: not so says the letters are not in the order given, so they must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone insists the work was indeed never printed, and is contradicted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not so' rearranges IT and INDEED.
explanation.definitionFit: Edited once meant published, so an unedited, unissued manuscript is one never put out in print.

clue.text: Understood, as people did in meeting

explanation.surface: People grasped the point at an assembly.
explanation.definitionFit: If you gathered something you inferred it, and people who assembled together for a meeting came together.

clue.text: Having a pound in rocky coast? Mining could be

indicators.note: in tells us the enclosure is placed inside the reworked letters of coast
rocky means unsteady or shaken, so the letters of coast are jumbled

parts.note: a pound for animals is a pen, an enclosure

explanation.surface: A coastline with an animal enclosure, and a question of whether mining happens there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rocky' jumbles the coast's letters and 'in' puts the enclosure within them. 'pound' looks like money, but it is an animal enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: Opencast mining is extraction from an open surface pit rather than underground shafts.

clue.text: Side view

explanation.surface: Two words meaning a profile seen from one direction.
explanation.definitionFit: An aspect is one face or side of a building or problem, and also an outlook or prospect seen from a place.

clue.text: Some read items fully, others simply a passage

indicators.note: some means a portion, so only part of the words read items is taken, running across the word break

explanation.surface: Some people read every item thoroughly while others just read a short extract.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes a run of letters from 'read items'; 'fully, others simply' completes the surface and gives no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An adit is a horizontal entrance tunnel into a mine.

clue.text: Put faith in the act that conveys property

parts.note: to put faith in someone is to trust them
a deed is an act or action

explanation.surface: Believing in the legal document that hands an estate over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the act' reads as part of the legal phrase, but it supplies DEED on its own; the definition is the closing description of what the document does.
explanation.definitionFit: A trust deed is a legal document transferring an estate to trustees to hold on others' behalf.

clue.text: Middlesex, I learn, in part is cut off

indicators.note: in part says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone learns that the old county of Middlesex has been isolated.
explanation.walkthrough: Middlesex is a former English county, now absorbed into London. The answer spans the end of 'Middlesex' and the following 'I'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone banished from home is shut out or separated from it, which is what being in exile means.

clue.text: Greek I had in the frame!

parts.note: I had contracts to I'd, written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A Greek man exclaims that he had something framed.
explanation.definitionFit: A grid is a framework of crossing bars, like the frame of a grating.

clue.text: Drink flowing, we hear, in, riverside rendezvous

parts.note: a liquid that flows freely is runny

indicators.note: we hear says the drink is pronounced, and the spelling entered differs

parts.note: mead is an old drink made from honey

explanation.surface: A drink pouring at a meeting place by a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' turns MEAD into MEDE by sound. Runnymede is the Thames meadow where King John met the barons in 1215 to seal Magna Carta.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous meeting between king and barons took place on this meadow beside the Thames.

clue.text: The Royal Engineers merit refurbished galley

indicators.note: refurbished means done up anew, so the letters are put back together in a new order

parts.note: RE is the abbreviation for the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army

explanation.surface: Army engineers deserve credit for restoring an ancient boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refurbished' rearranges RE plus MERIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A trireme was an ancient warship rowed by three banks of oars, a type of galley.

clue.text: Cancelled, finished, hurt?

parts.note: an event cancelled is off
finished means ended

explanation.surface: A list of reactions to an abandoned event.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone hurt by a remark has taken umbrage, which is to feel insulted.

clue.text: Do I in arrangement behind flower get a small item in space?

indicators.note: behind says the scrambled letters come after the flower in the answer

parts.note: an aster is a daisy-like garden flower

indicators.note: in arrangement says the letters of do I are rearranged, as in flower arranging

explanation.surface: Someone arranging flowers asks whether they will win a small prize.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' tempts as something that flows; here it is the bloom, and the jumbled letters come 'behind' it.
explanation.definitionFit: An asteroid is a minor planet, a small rocky body orbiting the sun.

clue.text: Description of finely woven articles that shine out in this paper

indicators.note: in places the reworked letters within the newspaper's initials

parts.note: the clue appeared in the Financial Times, abbreviated FT

indicators.note: out here means out of order, so the letters of shine are mixed

explanation.surface: A newspaper feature on stockings that gleam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' turns SHINE into ISHNE, which goes 'in' FT, this paper being the Financial Times.
explanation.definitionFit: Fishnet is an open-mesh fabric used to describe tights or stockings with a fine woven net pattern.

clue.text: Take to this to call to account

definitions.text: Take to this to call to account

parts.words: Take to this to call to account
parts.note: the clue is the idiom with its last word replaced by this, asking what completes the phrase for a reprimand

explanation.surface: Instructions on bringing someone to book.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill 'this' to complete the phrase 'take to ...', meaning to rebuke.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone to task is to rebuke them, holding them to account for something.

clue.text: What could be called left off polish?

indicators.note: off says one letter is taken away from the word before

parts.note: in poker you call someone's bluff, so a bluff is what could be called

explanation.surface: A question about what to call leftover polish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'called' points to the poker phrase 'call a bluff'; 'off' then removes L for left.
explanation.definitionFit: To buff a surface is to rub it until it shines, as with a soft cloth.

clue.text: Spot the flaw?

explanation.surface: A spot-the-difference puzzle asking you to find what is wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: A blemish is a mark on the skin and also a defect or imperfection in something.

clue.text: Shaky ride, e.g. relatively anxious

indicators.note: shaky means wobbling and unsteady, so the letters are shaken into another order

explanation.surface: A bumpy trip makes someone more nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shaky' rearranges RIDE and EG.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgy means nervous, so the comparative means more nervous than before.

clue.text: Be off with you! (Be a bird?)

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird

explanation.surface: Someone tells a pest to go away, then wonders whether to be a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket gives the wordplay: BE, A and TIT, a small bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Telling someone to go away or clear off is an order to leave immediately.

clue.text: English — a light for all?

parts.note: a Very light is a coloured signal flare fired from a pistol

explanation.surface: An English lamp that can be used by everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: A Very light is a flare named after its inventor; the word is not the adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: Every and all both mean each one without exception, as in 'every person' or 'all people'.

clue.text: Run off hastily in an informal way

definitions.text: Run off hastily in an informal way

parts.words: Run off hastily in an informal way
parts.note: the clue describes a colloquial word for fleeing in a hurry, the second half saying it is slang

explanation.surface: Fleeing quickly and casually.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition and the tag 'in an informal way' are one description: a slang verb for scarpering.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a colloquial American verb for bolting or scattering at speed.

clue.text: Take top off pattern. That's enough

indicators.note: take top off says to remove the first letter of the word, the top in a down clue

parts.note: a sample or specimen serves as a pattern of the whole

explanation.surface: Removing the top of a design and declaring it sufficient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take top off' removes the S from SAMPLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ample means plentiful, more than sufficient.

clue.text: A day with the car and one gets cattle to market

parts.note: Rover is a British make of car

explanation.surface: A day out in the car, and someone herding cows to sale.
explanation.walkthrough: ROVER is a British car make.
explanation.definitionFit: A drover is a herdsman who drives livestock along roads to sale.

clue.text: Locate exactly a trifling thing

explanation.surface: Finding precisely where something tiny is.
explanation.definitionFit: To find a precise position is to pinpoint it, and a tiny or negligible thing is a mere pinpoint, as small as a pin's tip.

clue.text: One associated with a Twist

parts.note: Twist is the hero of Dickens's Oliver Twist, so the clue wants a character linked to him

explanation.surface: Someone connected with a dance craze or a cocktail garnish.
explanation.walkthrough: The Artful Dodger is the young pickpocket who befriends Oliver in Dickens's novel. 'Twist' has a capital to point to the novel, not a dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The Artful Dodger is the street thief who takes Oliver to Fagin, so he is closely tied to Twist.

clue.text: Animal disease caused by a fluke

definitions.text: Animal disease caused by a fluke

parts.words: Animal disease caused by a fluke
parts.note: a fluke is both a stroke of luck and a parasitic flatworm that infests the liver of livestock

explanation.surface: A livestock illness that struck by chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by a fluke' seems to mean by luck, but the liver fluke is the parasite that causes this ailment in sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: Liver rot in flocks is caused by the parasitic flatworm infesting their livers.
